title: Churn prediction (Telco customer churn)
problem: For a subscription business, which modeling choices give a reliable churn-risk ranking, and do deep tabular models beat simple ones on this kind of data?

understanding.unit: one customer at the snapshot date

pitfalls: Forbidden: `customerID` (identifier; target-encoding it inflated ROC-AUC from 0.82 to 1.00 in PIT-004)
Open issue: the real prediction timestamp and outcome window are not recorded in the public data
solution: Primary metric: ROC-AUC and average precision

title: Places: values over a map
problem: How much does a random split flatter a model of values over a map (prices across a city), where nearby places are alike, against a split that keeps whole blocks of places on one side? The answer decides when the places kind splits by blocks and how large they are.

understanding.moment: when the place is listed: its location, size, rooms and age known

solution: Primary metric: MAE, on held-out blocks of places

title: Tabular classification (HyperAck and public benchmarks)
problem: How do we build the most accurate *honest* classifier for tabular business data, and which steps (leakage control, feature engineering, algorithm choice, tuning, calibration) actually move the score?

understanding.moment: when the order is created, before dispatch

pitfalls: Forbidden: `final_customer_fare`, `final_biker_fare` (only known after the outcome)
solution: Primary metric: ROC-AUC, with recall at the operating threshold

title: Tabular regression
problem: How does DCLab predict a number from one table (minutes, a price, an amount) without a post-outcome column in it, and how much does a wrong split or a kept leak flatter the error? The answer decides which columns the regression kind keeps out and which split it reports.

understanding.moment: when the row is created, before its outcome

solution: Primary metric: MAE, with the training median as the baseline

title: A discount campaign
problem: who buys because of the offer (an uplift replica), randomised and observational
pitfalls: Who buys is not who responds: Loyal customers with many past purchases buy often with or without the offer; the offer changes the minds of young app users only. A model of who buys when offered targets the loyal ones and wastes the budget.

Not every campaign is an experiment: In the observational version the marketing team sent the offer mostly to customers with many past purchases: the arms barely overlap, and a difference between them is not the offer's effect. The planted responsive segment and every row's true uplift are in ``facts`` (for judging only).

title: Flat prices in a city
problem: a regression where places cluster
pitfalls: Neighbours are alike: Each district has its own price level, a smooth field over the city that no column but the coordinates carries. A random split puts a flat's neighbours in training and the flat in the test: the score measures how well the model remembers the district, not how it prices a flat in an area it has not seen.

Places cluster: Flats come in neighbourhoods of different density; a block of the city is the honest unit to hold out. The price field's centres and the correlation range are in ``facts`` (for judging only).

title: Customers
problem: with three planted behaviours and noise: groups with no outcome to predict
data: The behaviours: bargain hunters (frequent small baskets, mostly on discount, through the app), loyal premium buyers (regular large baskets, little discount, in store) and occasional visitors (rare, medium baskets, recently inactive). A tenth of the customers follow none of them. ``region`` and ``signup_week`` carry no behaviour: a segmentation that splits on them is splitting noise. The planted behaviour of each row is in ``facts`` (for judging only), and so is a later outcome (``renewed``) that differs by behaviour.
pitfalls: no ground truth in the table
skewed amounts that dominate an unscaled distance
a number of segments that looks better with more groups but does not come back when the data is resampled

title: A delivery-fraud challenge
problem: a ride table and a separate sample of known frauds (package 15.1)
data: Shaped like a real hiring challenge the owner gave DCLab (its data is confidential and never used here). The person gets two files and the question "find the bikers' and customers' fraud".
pitfalls: The labels are in another file, and the right key is the order: Joining the sample on (account, biker) marks every ride of a fraudulent biker for that account: there are only three accounts, so the coarse join inflates the labels many times over.
The labels are partial: The sample holds only some of the planted frauds; the rest of the table is unlabelled, not clean. A few sample rows belong to an account that is not in the table at all.

One column name means two things: ``sender_phone`` is the sender's phone in the table, but in the sample it holds the *receiver's* phone (it equals the biker's phone for self-dealing rides). The sample's fares also disagree with the table's.
Rows cluster on entities: The frauds come from a few bikers; a random split lets a model recognise the biker.
The signal is behaviour: A fake ride ends a few metres from its pick-up, at a drop-off the same biker returns to. The raw columns (a fare, a coordinate) carry little of it.

One kind of fraud is invisible in the table: Self-dealing (the biker delivers to his own phone) shows only through the receiver's phone, which the table does not have. Cancelled rides have no biker. Some orders have two or three drop-offs (terminals), each a row.

title: Delivery time
problem: estimate how many minutes an order will take, when it is placed
pitfalls: A heavy tail and a cap: Times are right-skewed, and the source system stores anything above 60 minutes as 60: the top value is a cap, not a measurement (censoring), so squared error chases it and the tail is unknown.
The target can be recomputed: ``delivered_at`` minus ``order_time`` is the target, to the minute; and ``courier_rating`` is given after the delivery. Neither exists when the order is placed.
A few impossible values: Some distances are negative (a sign error in one data feed).
Restaurants repeat: Each restaurant has its own preparation speed: grouping by restaurant shows how a model does on a new one.
Weather goes missing more in storms: Missing ``weather`` happens more often on slow days, so missingness speaks.

title: A fraud programme
problem: rides, accounts and a partial list of confirmed cases, with three kinds of fraud planted (package 24.6)
data: A courier platform wants to find the fake rides and fake orders its bikers and customers make. It has a ride table, the table of its customer accounts and a list of the cases an investigator confirmed; a team can review a small share of the rides each day. The problem is several problems that depend on each other, and each kind of fraud is visible to one of them only: * **Fake delivery marks.** A few bikers mark a ride delivered without moving: the ride ends within metres of where it began, in a minute or two, for a normal fare. The behaviour of the ride gives it away; no other table is needed
pitfalls: The scale is chosen for power, not for a result: with few fraudulent bikers a bootstrap over bikers is too wide to tell a real gain from chance, so the replica has 14 rings and 28 marker bikers, each with few rides (calibrated on the seeds 10 to 15; the acceptance runs the seeds 0 to 2, which the calibration never saw).
Invented data: a score on it says whether the decisions are sound, never how a model would do on real rides.

title: Machines with sensors
problem: alert before a failure
data: Hourly readings of temperature, vibration and pressure for each machine. Failures are rare. In the two days before a failure, vibration creeps up and temperature drifts: the warning signs. Machines differ in their normal level, so a reading is unusual only against the machine's own past. After a failure the machine is down for a day.
pitfalls: The future in a window: A window that reads one hour past its end sees the failure itself.
Rows are not incidents: Thousands of quiet windows and a few dozen failures: accuracy per row says nothing; count the failures caught, how early, and the alerts per machine-day it costs.

Machines differ: A threshold on raw vibration flags the loud machines all the time; a change against each machine's own level finds the warning signs. The failure times are in ``incidents``; ``facts`` keeps the warning length (for judging).

title: Product reviews
problem: whether a review is negative, from its text and the fields that come with it (a text + tabular replica)
pitfalls: The signal is in the words: The structured fields (category, price, the reviewer's past reviews) carry little; a model on them alone is weak. Words decide.
A reply written after the review: ``shop_reply`` is the shop's answer, written after the review and its rating: an apology gives the outcome away, and it does not exist when the review arrives.
An identifier: ``review_id`` is unique per row.
Negative reviews are the minority: About one in five; accuracy flatters.

title: Ride pricing
problem: a courier is offered a fee for a ride and accepts it or not (a pricing replica, shaped like the first part of a delivery challenge: choose the fee)
data: Two versions of the same market: * ``varied=True``: the fee offered is the usual fee for the trip times a multiplier drawn at random (a pricing test), so the data can show how acceptance responds to the fee. * ``varied=False``: the fee is a fixed formula of distance and the hour, never varied on its own: the data cannot tell the fee's effect from the trip's, and a careful data scientist says so instead of drawing a curve.
pitfalls: Acceptance after the offer: ``accepted_at`` exists only when the courier accepted: it is a copy of the label.
The fee is a decision, not only a feature: Choosing it needs a model of acceptance by fee and a margin, not the best accuracy.

Edges: The best fee must be read within the fees tried. The truth (``facts``): acceptance is logistic in the log of the multiplier with elasticity ``ELASTICITY``, plus the trip's context; the margin per offer at multiple m is ``(m * usual_fee - cost) * P(accept | m)`` with the platform earning ``CUSTOMER_PRICE_FACTOR`` times the usual fee, so the best multiple can be computed exactly.

title: Images and long texts
problem: with planted labels and near copies (replicas for package 16.12)
data: ``shapes``: small grey images of a circle or a square (the label) at random places and sizes, photographed several times per scene with a little noise: the shots of one scene are near copies, so a random split puts one shot in training and its twin in the test. ``notes``: long support tickets whose label (urgent or not) depends on what the text says, written by authors with their own phrasing; a few tickets were pasted again by another author with a new first line: near copies across authors. With ``outcomes=True`` each ticket also has a ``topic`` (seven classes, from the phrase it was written
pitfalls: ``shapes``: small grey images of a circle or a square (the label) at random places and sizes, photographed several times per scene with a little noise: the shots of one scene are near copies, so a random split puts one shot in training and its twin in the test.

``notes``: long support tickets whose label (urgent or not) depends on what the text says, written by authors with their own phrasing; a few tickets were pasted again by another author with a new first line: near copies across authors.
Each item's scene or author is its source: folds must keep a source on one side.

title: A shop's customers, orders and support tickets
problem: which customers stop ordering in the 30 days after a cutoff (a several-tables replica)
pitfalls: Events after the cutoff: The question is asked on a date; a customer's orders and tickets after it are the answer, not a feature. Counting all of a customer's orders reads the future.
A snapshot taken at the end: The customer table was exported on the last day: ``last_order_date`` and ``lifetime_orders`` describe the customer at the export, not at any cutoff.
A join that repeats rows: ``addresses`` holds several rows per customer: joined as it is, it repeats customers.
Slowing down before leaving: Customers who stop ordering first order less often and open more tickets: window counts and trends see it; one total does not.

title: A shop's views and purchases
problem: which items to show each customer next
pitfalls: The future in the item table: ``lifetime_sales`` is each item's purchases over the whole log, the weeks after the recommendation moment included. Ranking by it looks excellent and cannot be done on the day.
Items that did not exist yet: New items keep arriving; an item added after the moment cannot be recommended at it, and a popularity count taken over the whole log would put the new hits on top.
Popularity is strong: A few items sell to everyone: every model must be compared with the most popular items, and with the items popular lately.
Taste: Each customer prefers a few categories: a model that learns it beats popularity on the customers who have a history.

title: Store demand
problem: daily units sold per store and product, forecast a week ahead
pitfalls: Known ahead, and not: ``on_promotion`` is planned weeks ahead: known at the forecast moment for the days forecast. ``rain_mm`` is the day's measured rain: it moves demand, but on the forecast moment it is not known for the days ahead (only a weather forecast would be). Using it is a leak that backtests at a random split hide.
A week's season: Weekends sell more: a model must beat the seasonal naive (the same weekday last week), not only the naive last value.
The future in a random split: Rows of the same series are ordered in time; a shuffled split lets lags of the future into training. Backtests must cut at origins and use only the past.
Short series: A few products start late: too short for a model of their own.

title: Subscription churn
problem: which subscribers cancel before their next renewal
pitfalls: A column written after the outcome: ``final_refund_amount`` is paid only when a subscriber cancels: it is close to a copy of the label and does not exist at renewal time.
An identifier: ``subscriber_id`` is unique per row; a model can memorise it and learn nothing.
Rows arrive over time: Subscribers sign up over two years and the cancel rate drifts upward: a random split mixes the future into training, the holdout should be the latest signups.
Accuracy flatters: About a quarter cancel: predicting "stays" for everyone is right three times out of four.

title: Subscription lifetimes
problem: how long until a subscriber cancels, when many have not cancelled yet (a time-to-event replica)
pitfalls: Right-censoring: Subscribers sign up over two years and the data ends on one day: a subscriber who signed up last month and is still active has a duration of one month and no event. Dropping such rows keeps the short lives and forgets the long ones; calling them cancellations ends lives that go on. Both make subscriptions look shorter than they are.

Counted during the follow-up: ``months_billed`` and ``tickets_so_far`` grow with every month a subscriber stays: they are not known at signup, the moment the forecast is made, and they predict the duration only because they measure it.

Rows arrive over time: The holdout is the latest signups, whose follow-up is short: a horizon is scored only where the follow-up reaches it. The true survival at each horizon and every row's true lifetime are in ``facts`` (before censoring), so a test can say which estimate, and which score, is honest; a solver never reads them.

title: Ticket routing
problem: route each support ticket to one of 12 teams when it is created
pitfalls: Tiny classes: Two teams receive about 0.3 % of tickets each: accuracy hides them, macro metrics and stratified folds do not; merging or a hierarchy is worth a look.

Columns written after the moment: ``resolved_by`` (the agent who closed the ticket, always from the handling team) is close to a copy of the label; ``first_response_minutes`` depends on the team's queue. Neither exists when the ticket is created.
Repeated tickets: About 2 % of rows are exact duplicates (a form submitted twice): a split can put copies on both sides.
Customers repeat: Customers open several tickets and keep to a few teams: grouping by customer is worth testing.
A team appears late: ``integrations`` starts in the last month, so a random split overstates how well it is learned.

title: Delivery fraud by bikers and customers (the owner's)
problem: Detect fraudulent rides by bikers and customers in one city's ride table; a small sample of known forged rides measures it.

understanding.target: A ride in the known fraud sample
understanding.labels: A sample of the cases found: positive-unlabelled

pitfalls: Joining the fraud sample on `order_request_id` gives **94 known fraud rides** out of 133,138 delivered rides (0.07 %, on 53 bikers). The original notebooks joined on (customer_id, biker). The table has only two customer ids, so that join produced 3,416 "frauds".
Fake rides end where they start (median 26 m against 323 m). The same biker returns to the same drop-off square again and again, and the fare per metre is extreme.

PU bagging is statistically tied with the top model. It has the best ROC-AUC (0.938) and the best recall at 1 % (63 %), it is built for positive-unlabelled data, and it is cheap to retrain. Rules run beside it to explain each alert and to raise a hard alert on self-dealing phones.
Joining the cases on the customer instead of the order turned 94 frauds into 3,416.
solution: Rules, anomaly detectors, supervised and positive-unlabelled models, compared on biker-grouped folds with a cluster bootstrap and paired tests
PU bagging chosen: tied with the best on average precision, best ROC-AUC, the labels being a sample

title: Insurance claim fraud
problem: Flag the motor claims most likely to be fraudulent so the investigation unit looks at them first.

understanding.unit: One claim at first notice of loss
understanding.target: The claim was later confirmed fraudulent by an investigator
understanding.moment: When the claim is filed, before any payment
understanding.labels: Only investigated claims have a verdict: most claims are unlabelled, not clean
understanding.action: Investigators review the top claims each week; a missed fraud is paid, a false alarm delays an honest customer

data: claims: date, policy, amount, injury flag, garage, witnesses
policies: start date, cover, past claims
parties: drivers, garages and lawyers shared between claims
pitfalls: Investigation outcome and payment amount are written after the moment: never features
Labels exist only where someone looked: positive-unlabelled, and the investigated set is biased toward what was already suspected
Rings share garages, phones and lawyers: a split by claim leaks the ring; split by time or by party group
Precision at the review capacity is the metric, not accuracy
solution: Rules and anomaly scores for the unlabelled claims, a classifier on the investigated ones, a graph of shared parties for rings
Split by filing date; report precision and recall at the weekly review capacity
workflow: Write the moment: what is known at first notice
Join parties and policies as of that date
Screen for leaks in the investigation and payment fields
Build the rules, the anomaly scores and the classifier
Compose on validation, read the holdout once at the review capacity

source.ref: public knowledge: claim fraud detection practice

title: Credit default at application
problem: Score each loan application for the risk of default in the first year, to approve, price or decline it.

understanding.target: Ninety days past due within twelve months of disbursement
understanding.labels: Known only for approved loans: declined applicants have no outcome (reject inference)
understanding.action: Approve, price or decline; a default costs the principal, a wrong decline costs the margin

data: applications: income, employment, requested amount, purpose
bureau: history as of the application date
pitfalls: Bureau data must be as of the application date, not refreshed later
Only approved loans have outcomes: the model learns the old policy's population
A twelve-month window: the latest applications have no complete outcome yet and must be left out of training
Protected attributes and their proxies need a fairness review
solution: Out-of-time validation (the latest complete cohort as holdout)
Calibrated probabilities: pricing needs the rate, not only the rank
Monotone constraints where the business expects them
workflow: Define the outcome window and drop incomplete cohorts
Holdout on the latest complete cohort

title: Retail demand for replenishment
problem: Forecast next week's daily units per store and product so the replenishment system orders the right amount.

understanding.moment: Sunday evening, for the seven days ahead
understanding.labels: Sales are known for every past day; stock-outs hide true demand
understanding.action: Orders are placed from the forecast; too low empties shelves, too high wastes fresh stock

pitfalls: A day with zero stock shows zero sales, not zero demand: censored
Promotions are known ahead; weather is not (only its forecast)
A shuffled split puts the future in training: backtest at origins
Beat the seasonal naive (same weekday last week) before claiming a model
solution: Global gradient boosting over lags known at the origin, promotions and calendar
Rolling-origin backtests; the error scaled by the seasonal naive
workflow: Build lags only from the past

title: Predictive maintenance on industrial pumps
problem: Warn maintenance a day or two before a pump fails, from its sensors.

understanding.target: A failure within the next 48 hours
understanding.moment: At the end of each hour
understanding.labels: Failures from the maintenance log; planned stops are not failures
understanding.action: Schedule a check; a missed failure stops the line, a false alarm costs a technician's visit

data: maintenance log with failure and repair times
pitfalls: A window that reads past its end sees the failure
Rows are not incidents: count failures caught, how early, and alarms per pump-day
Pumps differ in their normal level: compare each to its own past
After a repair the series resets
solution: Features against each pump's own baseline (change, trend), a classifier on windows
Split by time and by pump; report failures caught and alarms per pump-day
workflow: Align the log and the sensors
Fit and choose the alarm threshold on validation

title: Churn of business subscribers (SaaS)
problem: Find the accounts likely to cancel at their next renewal, so customer success can step in.

understanding.unit: One account, ninety days before its renewal
understanding.moment: Ninety days before the renewal date
understanding.action: Customer success calls the accounts at risk; a call costs an hour

pitfalls: Usage after the moment (the last ninety days) is the future
Cancellation requests and refunds are written after the outcome
An account renews many times: group by account so its renewals do not cross the split
Accounts that churned early never reach a ninety-day snapshot: survivorship
solution: Snapshots at a fixed lead time, grouped by account, split by renewal date
Precision in the top accounts the team can call
workflow: Build one snapshot per renewal at the lead time
Features from usage before the snapshot

title: B2B lead scoring
problem: Rank new inbound leads by their chance to become a paying customer, so sales calls the best first.

understanding.target: Became a customer within six months
understanding.labels: Known after six months; recent leads are still open
understanding.action: Sales calls the top of the list each day

pitfalls: Sales activity after creation (calls, meetings) is the future and the treatment
Open leads are not negatives: drop or wait for the window
Leads from one company repeat: group by company
solution: A ranker evaluated by precision at the daily call capacity
Time split by creation date
workflow: Holdout on the latest closed cohort

title: Support ticket triage
problem: Route each new ticket to the right team and flag the urgent ones from its text and form fields.

understanding.target: The team that resolved it; urgent or not
understanding.labels: The resolving team for every closed ticket
understanding.action: The ticket goes to the team's queue; a wrong route costs a transfer

pitfalls: Resolver, resolution time and closing notes are written after the moment
Tiny teams: macro metrics and stratified folds
Duplicate submissions cross the split
Text embeddings must be fitted on training tickets only
solution: Text with tabular fields; macro F1 and per-team recall
Group by customer to test generalisation
workflow: Encode the text on training folds

title: Delivery time estimate (ETA)
problem: Tell the customer at checkout how many minutes their order will take.

understanding.moment: At checkout, before a courier is assigned
understanding.labels: Every delivered order; cancelled ones have none
understanding.action: The promise shown to the customer; late orders cost refunds

data: order time, distance, restaurant, basket size
pitfalls: Delivered-at minus ordered-at is the target: any timestamp after checkout leaks it
Times above a cap are stored as the cap: censored
Restaurants differ: group by restaurant for new ones
Quantile error matters more than the mean for a promise
solution: Gradient boosting with a quantile loss for the promise
Time split; report MAE and the share of late promises

title: Ride price acceptance
problem: Predict whether a rider accepts the quoted price, to choose the price that balances acceptance and margin.

understanding.action: The price shown; a price too high loses the ride, too low loses margin

data: supply and demand at the moment
pitfalls: Acceptance time and the final fare are after the moment
Past prices were chosen by the old policy: the effect of price is confounded
A random experiment on price is worth more than any observational model
solution: A calibrated acceptance model; price effects only from randomised quotes or careful causal design
workflow: Separate the policy's choices from the effect

title: Product recommendations for a webshop
problem: Show each visitor a personal top ten of products they are likely to buy next.

understanding.target: The products bought in the next 14 days
understanding.moment: At the date of the recommendation
understanding.action: The top ten shown; a good list raises sales

pitfalls: A random split leaks the future: split by time
Popularity is a strong baseline that must be beaten
New products and new customers have no history (cold start)
solution: Recall and NDCG at ten on the next period, against popularity and recent-items baselines

title: Who to send a discount to (uplift)
problem: Send the voucher only to customers whose buying it changes, not to those who would buy anyway.

understanding.target: Bought within 30 days, with and without the voucher
understanding.labels: A random holdout group without the voucher
understanding.action: Send or not; a voucher to a sure buyer is wasted margin

pitfalls: Without a random control there is no uplift to learn
A response model ranks the sure buyers first: the wrong target
Evaluate with uplift curves (Qini), not accuracy
solution: Two-model or transformed-outcome learners on the randomised campaign
Qini on a holdout of the campaign

title: Unusual card payments without labels
problem: Surface the strangest payments of the day for an analyst, before any fraud is confirmed.

understanding.labels: None, or a few confirmed cases later
understanding.action: An analyst reviews the top list; their verdicts become labels

data: payments with merchant, amount, country, device
pitfalls: Unusual is not fraud: measure on planted or confirmed cases
Compare a payment to its card's own past, not to everyone
Feedback loops: the analysts only see what the detector shows
solution: Detectors chosen on planted anomalies of a validation period
A review list of the analyst's capacity; confirmed alerts become labels for a classifier later

title: Hospital readmission within 30 days
problem: At discharge, flag the patients most likely to come back within 30 days, for a follow-up call.

understanding.labels: Known 30 days later; transfers and deaths need rules
understanding.action: A nurse calls the flagged patients; a missed readmission costs a bed

pitfalls: Codes billed after discharge are the future
Patients repeat: group by patient
Death within 30 days is not a non-readmission
Sensitive data: names and identifiers never leave
solution: Grouped time split; calibrated risk; recall at the nurses' capacity
A fairness review across patient groups
workflow: Define the outcome with its exceptions

title: Electricity load forecast
problem: Forecast tomorrow's hourly load for each substation, for the dispatch plan.

understanding.action: Generation is scheduled from it; errors cost balancing energy

pitfalls: Use the temperature forecast available at 10:00, not the measured temperature
Daylight saving days have 23 or 25 hours
Holidays behave like Sundays
solution: Gradient boosting on lags at the origin, forecast weather and calendar, backtests at many origins

title: Employee attrition
problem: Estimate which employees may leave in the next six months, to plan retention conversations.

understanding.unit: One employee at a quarter's start
understanding.action: Managers hold a conversation; it must never be used to punish

pitfalls: Exit interviews and resignation dates are after the moment
Censoring: people still employed are not 'stayed forever'
Small teams: identifiable people; aggregate what is shown
Ethics: an advisory signal, never a decision
solution: A survival model or snapshots with a fixed window; report on the latest quarter

title: Revenue of a new store location
problem: Estimate yearly revenue of a candidate site before opening a store there.

understanding.action: Open or not; a bad site loses the fit-out

data: footfall, population and competitors around each site
pitfalls: Neighbouring stores share demand: a random split leaks the area; split by spatial blocks
Revenue after year one reflects the store's own success
Few stores: wide intervals
solution: Spatial-block cross-validation; intervals, not only a point estimate
